BY C. H. SPURGEON.

D HE age is on the stir. Some sadly compare it to "the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast np mire and dirt"; and the analogy certainly holds good to a very high degree. Others liken the period to the awakening days of spring, when all the pent-up forces bu::Qt, into action, and prophesy a season of growth and fruit. There is truth in this also, although the awakening energies are not all those of goodness, and caution asks the question, "What will the harvest be ? " In any ca•e, the constable of society cries roughly, "Move on"; and the throngs in the streets of Mansoul insist that everyone shall proceed one way or another. Virtuous advances, if possible; but advances, even if virtue be left behind : such is the restless demand of the time. Politics in a hurry takes to alliances which patriotism formerly forbade, and ventures upon stratagems which old-fashioned honesty would have condemned. Benevolence in a fever will not stay to consider possible failure, and assured hazard; but declares that the die is cast, and goes in for a vast experiment. Liberty, sick of her own sweets, turns to despotic power, as, at least in religion, the cure for her feebleness. Religion itself, weary of laborious advance, regards her holy scruples as frnpedimenta, and adopts the methods of the world, while her doctrinal teaching is left, like some ancient Cffisar's camp, to be viewed as a curiosity by this advanced generation. These are serious alterations; are they improvements?

Those who h_av~ no delight in unsettlement, and useless change, nro by no mrans ~nd11ferent spectators of the childish freaks of this lighthraded generation. As freBh developmmts appear, the question ari~es again ,md 11gain, "What next,?" and with thr enquiry comes the sigh: " 0 Lord, how long?·• Certain of us are distresstcd beyond measure by that which others enter npon with a light heart. To mention this is to bring upon such dissentienls a storm of ridicule. Our regrets cause no con\"ern to the changeful ones. Why should they? They de~pise the old fogies who cannot, like themselves, rush into the bogs after the jack-o'-lant~rn of progress. "Doctrine! " cry they, "Who cares for that f " C111lrng it "dopma," they make a football of it, and again they shout, "w·ho cares?" ,vithout w·aiting for an answer, they hurry for- Wlird in their infallible wisdom to e.xerciEe their liberality of spirit by scoffing at the ne.rrow-minrled orthodox. "Waters of a full cup arc wrung out to them." New teachings and new methods mar the peace of ct.urches which, for many generatiuns, ham held to the once-delivereJ. faith. The intrusion has been wanton and illegal; but what of that r Protests are of no avail: it usually suffices to answer them with a rneer. Where contempt would Ecarcely be prudent, the preteu9e of agreement is made to cover orer a fatal difference, and to give opportunity to stab the truth iu the back. All things appear to be regarded as fair in the conflict with old-fashioned believers: they are a kind of creature with whom no faith is to be kept, aud to whom no rights al'e reserved. No matter how venerable in yearl'I, profound in knowledge, or great iu usefulness a man m11y be, let him hold to· the old faith, and he has thereby forfeited every claim to regard. "He was the founder of the church." He has ruled it too long ! "Be lias been its principal pillar for many years." It is time that there was a change! "He i.~ gentlP, and of tender sp£rit. It is cruel to oppose him.'' Men cannot be considered; if thfy are opposed to modern progress, they must endure the ineritable ! This is the spirit of the new religion-the religion of '' humanity," the religion or "thought and culture." So to describe it is to give serious offence, but the dest:riptiou has been prored to be emµhatically true iu many iustances; and othertl will be forthcoming wi1 h cruel c~rtaiuty in due time. Is anything more precious given to us in the place of the doctrine which is said to be obsolete, and is therefore to be scouted? By no rue-,ns. The subEtitutes for Solomon's shields of gold are not made ot' diamond, but of brass, and that brass of a poor sort. The dishes of solid meat are removed from the table, and pottage of the most watery sort occupies the room-a pottage into which wild gourds have been i,;hred, so that there is "death in the pot." The results patent to all, in man}' cases, are the decay of piety, the death of prayer-meetings, the fn·quenting of theatres .. nd other places of amusement, lax morals, antl a general worldliness of life. Need we go far to find Nonconformist churches which will nerer be accused of Puritanism, but might trnthfully be called clubs for social, political, literary, and sportive purposes ? Of course, the provisiuu of amusement is judged to be laudable, aud by no rue~ns a thing nquiring to be defended ; while the holding of bazaar8, in which the etagc itself is left iu the rear, and Vanity Fair is 0utd,JDr:, is justified and c:ommended. We have "Institutes'' for youth,

the ahyss? It is cheering to. believe that many have of late been braced up, and are recovering their footing. Testimony for the gospel is clearer from many pulpits than it was wont to be; for which may God be praised ! In other cases the new Eystem has worked it,elf out; and, arouEed by the disastrous result, the people have returned to the truth which they once loved. The heart of the churches is in a great measure sound ; and when those who rule the hour are no longer able to silence the much-enduring people, there will be a return to the former beliefs, and this will be accompanied by a firmer adhesion to them in the future. Too much is it a fact that a clique is ruling, and the real voice of the people is unheard. Be that as it may, believers must look well to the foundations. We need to have the fundamentals laid continually; anri doctrines taken for granted must be once more Scripturally proved. More and more mu~t faith renounce dependPnce upon the arm of flesh, and cling tenaciously to the Lord and his Word, without the admixture of other reliances. Nothing is to be done but to continue " steadfast, unmoveable, al ways abounding in the work of the Lord." There is one gospel, and if that be preached in the power of the one Spirit, it must accomplish the purposes of God. God will raise up his own champions. In the way of his Providence he will fight for his own cause. This is all we desire. Party we must have none ; personal honour we must not consider; let truth become once more dear to Zion, and by whomsoever the Lord shall work the reformation, it sufficeth ns. If, for her sins, the present visible church shall be left to decline into dee.t.h, it will be a heavy heart-sickness to the faithful; but even then they have no reason to despair. Out of the stones of Jordan God can raise up children unto Abraham. His purposes fail not. The end of the book of history will show his hand, even if in some of its pages his name be not readily discernible. If he was honoured 'll"ho believed in Rome when her foes were within her walls, so shall he be who believes in the triumph of the faith when app!irently overcome by the subtlest of her adversaries. In the most disastrous hour of the march of the army of the Lord, when the Amalekites are smiting the hindmost, he will do well who will take his stand, and hold his ground, and resolve to die b~neath the arrows of ridicule rather than suffer harm to the ark of God. There is a faith which turns to flight the armies of the aliem. May we each one possess it now!

One summer day I climbed up from Pontresioa to the Beroina Hospice, and then, having seen the lakes, my wife end I wandered further on to a coign of ,antage, where, on the further side stretches before the eye a scene of inimitable beauty. The colour of the two lakes is different---one black, one white; so, too, is the character of the two sorts of men-one de:filt>d and blackened by sin, the other whiter than snow. Looking fnrther into the rna 1 ter, I noticed that the source of the two lakes differed. BY THEODORE L. CUYLER, D.D. OUNG people often a~k me the qnestion•, "Would it be right for Y me to go to the theatre? If not, then why not?" Those who propound these qnestions are not of the dissipated and dissolute class, but clean young mfm anrl maidens-too clean t0 be smirched b_y needless exposure to impure influences. That such rinestions are constantly raised is not snrprisinfr, for the playhouse is increasingly persistent in it~ demands on popular attention and patr,,nage. It fills a constantly-enlarging place in the daily journals. Thea, reii multiply more rapidly than churches in some of our great cities. Theatre-going increases more than church-going. The dcai walls are co,ered with pictorial representations of scenes and acturs in full dress (or in very little dress), and many of these arc! of snch disgusting in- Jecency that they deserve suppression by the public authorities. If the pictures be so shameless, what mast the originals be? Before our youthful inquirers become patrons of the playh11use, it is bnt fair th~t they should know ju,t what perils to their moral nature and their welfare as i,nmortal beings they are likely to encounter. First. The first peril is to purity of charader. Your eyes and ears nre windows and doors to the heart. ·what entera once never goes out. Photographs taken on the memory are not easily effaced or barned up; they stick there, and often become tempters and tormentors for a lifetime. "I'd l(ive my right band," said a Ctirigtian to me once, "if I could rub out the abominable things that I put into my mind when I was a. fast young man.'' Ile could not do it I neither will yon be able to efface the lascivious images or the impure words which the stage may photograph on your very soul. We do not affirm that every popular µlay is immoral, or that every performer is impnre, or that every play-goer is on. the scent for sensual excitements ; but the stage is to be estimated as a totality, and the whole trend of the average American stage i:1 hostile to heart-purity. The exceptions do not alter the rule. Nor have h"nest attempts to bring the stage up to a hie!h standard of moral purity b.,en SllCCessful. The experiment, once made in Boston, of so managing a theatre as to exclude e,ery indelicacy from the stage, and every notoriously improper person from the audience, ended in a. pecuniary failure. The puritaniu playhouse soon went into bankruptcy. The chief object of the manager is to make money; and if he can spice his e,enin~ catertainment with a plot that turns ou a seduction, or with a scene of sexual passion, or with a salacious exposure of physical beauty, the tern ptatiou is ,ery often too strong to be resisted. You must take the average stage as it i8, and not as you would like to have it. It is an institution which, 1f you patronize it, you become morally responsible for-as much as if you were to patronize a public library or a public drinking-saloon. As au institution it habitually ausexes worna11 by parading her in man's attire before a mixed audience. Too ofteu it exposes her in such a pitiable scantiness of any attire at all, that if yon saw your own siste1· in such a plight you would turn away your eyes in horror. Yet you propose to pay your money, through the box-offic,., to somebody el8e's sisters and daughters to ,iolate womanly delicacy for your entertainment. If " the daughter of Herodias" dances to please

)·011, then you are responsible for the <lance in its influence on both the dancer and your own moral sense. There is no evading-, before God, ~-on_r accountability for the theatre if you habitually rnpport it. What its rnfluence upon the average performer is appears from mo~t abundo.nt tc>st1mon,. Oae of the most celebrated actrc~ses of this time informell a frirnd o'. mine tha_t s)1e "e_nter,i a Lhcatrc only to enact her part, and has ,Ny litt.Je asrnc1at10n with her own profession." A converted actor 0nC"e said to me, while passing a pl:iyhouse in which he had often performed, "Behind those curtains lies Sodom." Although sorely pressed to return to his old business, he said he would starve sooner than go on the st~ge again. Mrs. Frances Kemble Butler-the last living repre- ~ent.at1vc of the most famous histrionic family of modern times-has in her old age emphatically condemned the stage. As an institution the American theatre tolerates sensual impurity in its performers, and presents scenes of impurity to its patrons. If you become one of its patrons, you go into moral partnership with the theatre. Sr>cond. It would be e. sufficient condemnation of the average playbou~e if it stimulates one evil passion. But other temptations lurk about it. There are dangerous associations to be encountered there. It is a prevalent habit with young people who attend the theatre to remain nntil a late hour amid the excitement of the play@, and then to finish off with a midnight supper or a wine-drink at some neighbouring restaurant. To this perilous practice a young lady of my acquaintance owed her downftill, Long after sensible people have laid their heads on their pillows the habitues of the theatre are apt to be adding a second scene of dissipation to the first one. It must be pretty hard work for a Christian to finish up such an evening's experience with an honest prayer for God's blessing. That is indeed e. poor business and a poor pleasure on which we cannot with a clear conscience ask our heavenly Father's approval. Certainly there are enough innocent, wholesome, and beneficial recreations without venturing into the dangerous almosphere of the playhouse. That is a dear-bought pleasure which involves even a risk to the immortal soul. Third. Another peril of the theatre arises from the fascination whi'clt it too often engenders. Like wine-drinking, it becomes an appetite, and a -very greedy appetite. To gratify this growing passion f.,r the playhouse tens of tl.10usands of young peoµle most profusely squander their money and their time. Other and purer recreations become tame and insipid. Even the entertainments of the stage become dull unless they are spiced with new excitements to the passions. Wholesome pleasures cease to please, just as a brandy-drinker ceases to be satisfied with cold water or a cup of coffee. It is not recreation, but stimulation-and a very dangerous sort of stimulation too-that you will be after when you become enslaved by the fascinations of the stage. My Joung friends, be assured that no sagacious employer ever chooses a clerk, or an accountant, or any other employe, the sooner because he is a theatre-goer. No sensible man is apt to select the companion of his heart ;,nd home because she is a frequeuter of a playhouse. No wise Christian mother wants her sons and daughters to go there. No pastor expects his youthful church members to go into that impure atmosphere without a terrible damage to their piety. I do not believe that the

that what is said of America will have much truth in it when applied to England ; but possibly there may he a little less force in it, and allowance may be made. At least, we hope so; hut we certainly sh~ll not go to see. We observe enough of the ill influence of the theatre without nearer acquaintance.-0. H. S.J

This trait of the negro was illustrateri in a recent triai, in Irontown, of a white man named Chambers for shooting another man. The most important witness was Frank Jenkins, a ne11ro, who was whitewashing a chicken-coop only a few feet away when the quarrel took place. When the lie was given, defendant went for his gun. " What did you do then ? " asked the cross-examiner. Witness : " I jes' went on whitewashing de chicken-coop." Cross-examiner : " But when the defendant appeared with his gnn, and it looked as if someone was going to get hurt, then what did yon do?" Witness: "I kept on whitewashing de chicken-coop.'' Cross-examiner : "When the first shot was fired, what did you rlo?" Witnefs : "Kept right on whitewashing-. It was none of my business; and whah I cum from, in Kaintuck, I learned not to interfere with two white gentlemen occupied in settling a question of honah. I jes' turned up one corner of de coop, and kept ou whitewashing." Cross-examiner : " Did you do anything when they removed the body?'' Witness: "Ye~, sah; kept on whitewashing dat chicken-coop." Even the just.ice was moved to smile by this uncommon display of a disposition to attend strictly to one's own business. [This comes to us from America; and there is a lesson in it, which may be wholesome if taken with a grain of salt. If Frank Jenkins could have saved a life, he ought to have left his hen-coop, and his whitewash, and it may have been a passive selfishness which kept him from so doing. Yet if he kept clear of the quarrel because he had nothing to do with it, and had no gun, and the two white rnffians would probably both have turned on him, he was wise to mind his own work. At any rate, in most cases, when we have no right nor reason to iuterrneddle, we had better go on with the chicken-coop. At the present moment, in controversies, religious and political, the ordmary worker had better go on with hi~ Master's work, and lea_ve the fighting to others. Brother, feed your sheep ; and as to wh!it this man or that may be called upon to do, the word may come home to you from your Lord," What is that to thee? Follow thou me."-C. H. S.J

Ko. IV.-SYDENIIAM.

I CASKOT even write the name of this, my next'mission-field, without flashes from the CryHal Palace lighting up the mind's eye, nnd recollections of my own dear home flooding the memory. But, when I found rny~elf at Sydenham, I wns, lllas ! as far as ever from Joseph Paxton's beautiful creation, and from, to my eyes, the still more lovely ""\Yestwood." Ytt, wherefore do I sigh" 11las !"? It is surely better to be in the rath of duty, though exile from home is involved, than to enjoy in unappointed places the fellowship of nearest friends. Besides, the banishment affects our bodies merely, for "Though sunder'd far, by faith we meet Around our common mercy-seat." The Sydenham of which I write is a suburb of the city of Christchurch, and the nearest approach to the Crystal Palace it affords is found in the glass verandahs with which many of its "stores'' are furnished. In -physical configuration too, this Sydenham is the antipodes of the other. Gipsy, Beulah, and Sydenham hills, with all the other glor_ious heights around the Palac:e, give place, in this case, to a monotonous l€vel, relieved only by the Port Hills, some six miles distant, and Ly a range-of snow-capped mountains, perhaps forty miles away. Moreover, lhis Sydenham is not an aristocratic neighbourhood. It is populated for the moss part by the working-classes-i.e., by those who labour with their hands. By the way, I am not sure that they ought to ham the monopoly of that most honourable title, "working-classes.'' Surely many of thorn who d, irn the pen instead of the plough, and l1arnmer their brains instead of nails, and delve in fields of literature rather than in cabbage-gardens, are of the working-class as well. Many of them have longer hours, I know, than the so-called labouring-man, and some of them get hardly more remuneration; and they are labourers too, nnduubtedly, a!Lhough not "horny-handed sons of toil.'' But these S5denham people are, for the most part, workers in the ordinary acceptation of that term; the toilers and moiler11, on whom, to an extent so large, deµends the well-being of the body politic. There are few, if any, titled folk thereabouts. Some" professors" there may be, but they are of the tom.o: ial art; and the only "generals" I know of, resident in that district, are the general blacksmith and the general storekeeper. Right glad was I to have the opportunity of carrying the gospel to these busy beeE. Still is it true that Lhe poor have the gospel preached unto them. As a matter of fact, the poor get more of the gospel than the rich. The editor of 1'lte Sword and the Trowel once said, " We have plenty of ~ermons to the working-classes; 1 think we want some ser- 1JJous to the can·iage-classes. There is as much ignorance of the gospel awong tlie upper claoses as among the lower.'' Doubtless this iti so; bnd we all rejoice in those whom Uod has raised up to bear the good

She is, however, in the good handJ! of three earnest brethren who are steering bn from a lee-shore. Not inappropriately, the chief of the trio is named Marriner. May he prove a ma~ter mariner! He will have earneci that proud distinction if he and his mates succeed in weathering the cape on which it seemed possible the good ship might strike. This they will, doubtless, do; for though the crew is a comparatively small one, all hands are on deck, and an earnest., hopeful spirit. animates them ell. Good work bad been done before the Evangelist arrived, and a Reries of preparatory meetings h11d blessed the banners and whetted the swordJ! uf the faithful soldiers. There seemerl every prospect of success. From so large a. population large congregations would be gathered, composed of the sort, too, whose minds are most open to gospel truth. So we judged, and with great hopes unfurled the flag. But an unexpected 11indrance arose. Another battle was about to rage. On or about the same date commenced the great labour strife, and all men's heart3 were full_ of wonder and anxiety abont the struggle between capital and labour. Every night of the week some labour-meeting drew many away, and the strike absorbed the attention of all classes and conditions of men. Only on Sunday evenings conld we secure a large attendance. Nevertheless, the seed was sown, and the reaper hud some little work to do, too, thank God! We were delighted to learn that certain waverers had been stablished, some wanderers restored, and others, whose lamps were burning low, had them cleaned and trimmed, and charged with fresh oil. Moreover, the believers were welded together in the warm glow of a united effort to rescue the perishing. At one of the meetings, a note was handed to me, in which the writer (a widow), after acknowledging much ble8sing received throul!h one of r.he discourses, sent a message to the Evangelist's father. Can I do better than convey it to him through the columns of his own magazine ? It runs as fo11ows :-" Will you please tell your honoured father how much good his book, Morning by Morning, has done me. I have passed through deep waters, How oflen that book has cheered me ! Long may the Lord spare him, and use him for his glory ! " The Sydenham series over, we had to undertake .! LONG JOURNEY, and a not nneventful one. It looked as though we were not to carry out our programme. The crews of the coastal, as well as of the intercolonial boats, bad by this time been called out, and t~e ordi_nary time-table of the steamers wus quite suspended. So unlikely did_ 1t appear that we could get away, that I arranged to condul:t a sernce at the Christchurch B11ptist Church on Wednesday evening. T~at very evening a boat sailed, so my services had to be dispensed with, and

by six o'clock l and my "first mate" were oa hoard the s.s. " ,vnn11lm," honnd for Wellington. Onr next fi"!ld was Nelson, whitlwr we hoped to find another steamer going from Wellington. We could not expect to rear.h the formPr place 011 Thtir8day (whea we were due), but thought it barely possible we might arrive ere the next Lord's-day. Slippmg away in the darkness, without sounding the usual whistle~. we were not rnbjected to the hootings with which the unionists had been saluting the "blackleg" crews. We thanked God fot· a fair wind, and took courage. But long ere the next day dawned we discovered, like Peter, that the winds and the waves were boisterous, and our diminutive craft tossed about like the proverbial nutshell. The wind was still fair, but it had increased to the propo1·tio11s of at least "half a gale." Though b_v this time I may reckon myself a bit of a" salt," I confess I prefer Paddy's hurricane to even half a gale. In the former case, you know, the wind blows straight up and down the mast! Towards afternoon we found ourselves in calmer water, and hastening on deck, I looked around for the familiar landmarks of Wellington harbour. But they were nowhere to be seen. Presently the case was made plain. We were steaming up Queen Charlotte's Sound, and making for the town of Pictoo, where the captain wished to report himself by wire to Wellington. The prudent commander would not ventnre across Cook's Straits with an unaccustomed crew, and a small pressure of steam (for the firemen were novices), especially as the weather threatened to be thick on the lee-shore or the North Island. All hopes of reaching Nelson even hy Sunday were now taken away. It would probably be a day or two before we could venture out again, and when we did reach Wellington we would have to cross the Strait➔ a!?ain. What a wind was raging! How it swept down the gorges of the Sonnd, as through funnels, dense clouds of snowy spray flying before the besom of each blast ! '· One would think the deep to be hoary," or even that it boiled like a pot, had it not been so excruciati1111ly cold. Slowly we steamed, in the very teeth of this gale, until we reached the head of the Sound, and the town of Picton. It was now that it dawned upon ns that this storm was for the furtherance of the gospel. Had we reached Wellington, we could not have made Nelson belore the Sabbath, and now we were still on the Sauth Island (so is Nelson), with a coacl1 road to our destination. Bat, unfortunately, the coacb. was to leave Blenheim (some thirty miles from Picton) at G.45 next morning, and no vehicle was available to take ns to Blenheim overnight. So we slept at Picton, or rather, tried to. We should have had a better ch,mce of sleep at Bedlam than at Lhe Pier Hotel. Whether they were unionists, or "free labourers," or escaped lunatics, I know not, but certain it is that until two in the morning a yelling, shouting, singing (?), and, of course, drinking crowd, held high carnival beneath our dormiwry. Such are the peculiar views of pleasure which some men hold, while tbo,e who do not share them have to endure their well-nigh demoniacal din. The 8 o'clock train took us as far as Blenheim, where we met a former deacon of the Auckland Tabernacle. That same day, soon after noon, we set out in a special buggy, with two stout horses, and a young but able Jehu, on our drive ofover eighty miles. Right gaily we tripped it at the first, for the road was good, and the sun bright, and the animals

fre~h. 'fhe way 'lrns lcvcl--on a gloriously-fertile plain-till the wide bed of a river, whose name is of the unpronounceable order, had heen crossed. Then we wound op a lovely valley, with sheep upon the bills on either side. How often I wondered if this or that one would ever figure in The Sword and the Trowel, amongst the gifts to the orphans, as-" The New Zealand Sheep!" I could wish that more of them met with such distinction. It is only meet they should. After driving for, say, three hours, we passed through the township of Havelock, and remembered that Christian hero from whom it takes its name; as also Deacon Wm. Olney, whose son Herbert commenced his New Zealand career in this same spot. The evening was fast closing in when we pulled up at a wayeide inn, known as The Pelorns Hotel. We were in the very centre of Canvas Town, whose importance can be judged from the fact that it consists (so far as we could tell) of the bo~telry aforenamed, a smithy, and a church. 'l'he inn was of a humble sort, but it proved a Paradise in comparison to the pandemonium at Picton. Never was bread sweeter, nor chop more savoury, nor sleep more sound, for we were hungry and weary. The ground was white with frost next morning (Saturday) when we rnonnted our trap again, behind the same faithful steeds. And what a drive we had that day ! Our devious road led us over two mountain ranges, and along two heavily-timbered valleys. There was plenty to interest us en route. Trees, and ferns, and watercouraes, and creepers, and mosses, and native birds, and Californian quail, kept eyes and ears ever occupied. Of course, the way was rough in parts, and the inevitable back-aches and cramps preyed upon us. Bnt jolt@, and jars, and aclies were more than compensated for by the lovely views, and the freeh hill-air. Habitations were few and far between. Occasionally we descried one in a place as inaccessible as a lady's pocket. Presumably, there is a way to both. Once we looked down in a place called Happy Valley, where a miserable habitation, and not a blade of grass, contradicted the name. Only once did we tarry, and then but for forty minutes. Surely it speaks well for New Zealand horseflesh that our nags, though of course leg weary, seemed not unduly tired even when the journey was accomplished. About three of the clock, when some six miles from Nelson, we de~cried a figure, which was by no means unfamiliar, approaching us on horseback. The Rev. T. Bray, who once assisted in the work at Auckland-now Pastor of the Nelson Baptist Church-had come thus far to meet us. In another hour we were heartily welcomed by his worthy wife, and happily located in their cosy manse. So, despite th" storm ; nay, by means of it, we were in readiness to begin the Nelson Mission up to date, though we had miased the preparatory meetings. Extra expense and fatigue had been incurred, but we had good cause to be glad that by stre,s of weather we bad been compelled to travel overland, by what may well be called a " war-path," since Picton, Blenheirn, Marlborough, Havelock, and Nelson, are the names of the places and provinces through which we journeyed. We, too, were soldiers, but of a nobler warfare.

As our friend still remains a member of the ch~rch at the Tabernacle, Costers' Hall may still be reckoned as one of its outposts, although it is in all respects an active ~orking church, carrying on its operations quite independently. The aim b~s been, fr_om the first, to make converts; and then to emplo_v them m aggressive work among people of their own order. The result bas bee_n the gathering of a_ large and prosperous company, a large proportion of whom engage with ardour in Sunday-school, Bible-class, and other branches of service. Mr. W. J. Orsman is now to be reckoned among veterans in Christian enterpri~e; for in 1891 it will be thirty years since he commenced work i~ Golden Lane. What changes have come over that notorious locality smce 1~61, and over London generally; but as a Christian teacher, it is Mr. Orsman's happiness to be just where he was at the outset. As be himself remarks:- " Like the lighthouse we are not given to change, and friends can still find ns at the same blessed voluntary work which we commenced in 1861, in the Golden Lane and Boxton Christian Mission. Very few of our earlier co-workers remain, and we count it a special privilege to be still 'giving light, and saving life.' We make no compromise with the devil; but in our encounters with sin we adopt the military command-' Stnke hard, and strike quickly.' True religion does not make ns empty sentimentalists, but real, honest, devoted servants of the King" of kings. We 1ike reality, and leave all that savours of pretence or affectation to the theatre. Our surroundings call for warmth and entbnsiasm, hence we leave coldness and dulness outside. We love life, ::i.nd so banish the lifeless to the churchyard. Our place in the church of God is not to be exhibition11l, hut useful. Activity is the order of the day at Costers' Hall : we are all at it, and always at it, and we do onr best to make everything hearty, homely, and happy.'' Situated about a mile away from the former quarters in Golden Lane, Casters' Hall, with its thirty-two rooms, in addition to the essemblyroom, capable of accommodating 800 persons, is regarded by the costers, street-traders, and others, as their O\'l"n institution. There, without charge, they can have warm and well-lighted rooms for club meetings and other business purposes ; and occasionally a gathering of a wore festive character may take place. The chief work is of 11nother kind, however ; and this includes the Sunday services, the Sunday-schoolthe scholars of which throng the entire building-the Bibl~-readings, and prayer-meetings of the week, &c. These are all well attended ; and Mr. Orsman is able to say that "many spiritually dead and barren lives have beeorne living and fruitful by the grace ot God." There are also eveniug classes, Jee:tures, and a free library for such as desire to improve their educati, ,n. Then come temµerance and thrift; so that, altogether, uroarly forty distine:t meetings are held at the hall during tbe week.

This winter the breakfasts to famishing Board-school childrPn who would otherwise go fa~ting to Fchool, will be continued; whil~ the Irish stew, at 11, nominal charge, will, as in former years, be served out to needy people. By retiring from his position in the General Post Office a few months

ago, Mr. Orsman entered upon quite a new phase of his busy life; for hardly was he released from the Queen's service, than he was elected upon the London County Council. In conuection with this body he will do good service, for, as he says : "Once in the Council, we found plenty of congenial and useful work

present serving on the following committees :-Housing of the Working Cla~ses ; LunHtic Asylums ; Parks and Open Spaces; Bird and Animal Life in the Parks; Corporate Property, Charities and Endowments; London Water Supply, Markets, and Sanitary and Special Pnrposes. Our large experience of the needs of the Metropolis should enable us to render useful service on the above committees." Apart from the County Council, Mr. Orsman has at present two important enterprises in band, which will prove of great benefit to the poor when completed. One is the purclrnse of a suitable building for a Seaside Home on the South Coast, which, through the generous gifts of two friends, is likely foon to become an accomplished fact ; the other being the erection of dwellings in London for the accommodation of the poorest of the wage-earning clas,es. Our friend writes : - " It is well known that the substantial sanitary Model Dwellings now erected in many district:,,, are t.oo expensive for those whose earnings are uncertain, and rarely exceed 10/- a week ; yet~ is a numerous class almost beyond computation. It comprises joboing-men, seamstresses, hinndry and charwomen, widows, besides invalids and others who are kept out of the workhouse by the assistance of relatives and friends. Such persons now pay from 20 to 40 per cent. of their income for bare walls, with often insanitary accommodation, which is being rapidly condemned by the London County Council, and must shortly disappear." To remedy all this, Mr. Orsrnan proposes to put up, by way of experiment, on a cleared Fpace obtained from the London County Council, a building containing 100 rooms, to be let from a shilling to halt-a-crown a week, according to size. This cannot, of course, be made selJ~pa} ing; but one friend has promised £2,000, and if £8,000 can be obtained lrom others, the scheme can be completed. Thm, this comprehensi,e Mission continues on its way, carrying on its ordinary work, and developing new enterprises. Contributions to the ordinary fund, or otherwise, can be sent to Mr. W. J. Orsman, Milton House, Shacklewell Green, N.E., while parcels of cast-off clothing, &c., Ehonld be H:nt to Co~ters' Hall, Hoxton, London. Mr. Orsman is thus one of many volunteers who have ,:!iven time and energy to the work of improving the poor of London. We live in fastmovrng timf-s, howe,er, ia which "e find one proposing to set all things right by means of his Salvation Army. Sensational experimental schemes are, nevertheless, more likely to disappoint thoEe who embark in them than to he crowned with su1·cess; while nothing is more certain than that it would be a real disaster to the poor of London if support were withdrawn from the tried veterans, who have borne the burden and heat of the day, to indulge the foncy of sanguine adventurers, whose schemes in the main are quite as likely as otherwise to prove impracticable.

HE town of Duns, or Dunsc, thirteen miles from Benvir:k-upon- T Tweecl, and the chief town of Berwickshire, has been t.he birthplac:':! of several distinguished persons, and the scene of many remarkable events. Indeed, the whole district is full of objects of interest, ~nd n•plP-to with associations which carry us back to the early days of Christianit_y in these Islands. The followers of Columba, of Iona, invaded Northambria with the sword of the gospel, and many of the Angles were converted and civilized. They pursued their conquest down to Lindisf'arne, Whith_y, Durham, and York. Here Duns Scotu·s, the subtle Doctor, as the French named him, was born; and here a far greater than hE', Thomas Bostnn, the author of the " Fourfold State,'' long after first drew breath. The sight of an open grave and a mouldering corpse, in his native town, gave him, it is said, the first idea of the plan of his book, which is foll of the marrow of gospel truth. Perhaps a gre,1ter work than writinz the book, out of which thoughtful ministers might get no end of sermons, wai; the prominence he gave to the truths of the gospel in relation to the evangelization of the world. Associated with Ralph ancl Ebenezer Erskine, he first gav~ shape and direction to the evangelizing spirit which grew up io the bosom of the Scottish Church. In the brii(ht autumn (8th September) of 1817, Stephen Hislop was born, the youngest son of his father of the same name. The elder Stephen Hislop was one of a firm of three masons, or builders, who, while employing workmen, toiled with their own hands. Father ancl mother are described as "righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless." He went to school to one Dickson, then to Thomas Sheriff, nnd finally to Mercer, the accomplished Latin scholar. Under tbe second of these masters he is said to have learned two arts, which were afterwards ,ery usefol to him-the "statistical and the usefully artistic." Besides his parents, his minister, and teachers, "nature," we are told, "was his chief schoolmaster." Every holiday, every leisure hour, he was exploring the country round about; sometimes alone, sometimes with his elder brother, Robert; and, when bent on insect-hunting and the collecting of fossils, his most intimate friend and companion was a youth named Duns, now Professor Duns, of the New College, Edinburgh. There is still living in Duns an '' auld shoemaker," David Paterson, who has all his life heen a collector of insects, and of coins and medals. Dr. Smiles speaks of him as having the head of Jacob Boehme, and but one enemy in all the world-his poverty, which restricts his collections. David tells us that, when out on a fishing excursion, Robert Hislop had hooked a fine trout, and while Stephen was on the grass studying the beetles, the trout fell back into the stream, just abo,e the swirl of the mill. David, a boy in a pinafore, rushed in to catch it, and Stephen plunged in after him, and, with exceeding difficulty, rescued him from drowning. * Stephen Hislop, Pioneer Missionnr.v nnd Naturalist in Central India. By George Smith, C.I.E., LL.D. London: John Murray.

The picture of his boyh_ood and Jouth has been briefly drnwn by Dr. Dan1,1. When told tl1at his boy was al out to leave Scotland for Mission work in lndi11, tl1e father said, "Steephie frae a bairn was unco aulcl-farrand (sagacious), and aye sa guid.'' ' ' Stephen w11s not an early riser, but he lo,ed to sit up and read. His mother, who bpt a small shop, followed the good old rule •• early to hed, and early to rise." . S!1e li_ved for her so~s, of whom Stephen and Hoh~• t be?ome most d1stmgmshed. One evening, on her retiring, Stept1en said to her : - • "When "ill ) on be here in the morning ? " " At five," was her answer. "That will do," replied Stepher, "Oh, yes," said the mother dryly, "our Stephen's a grand riser at night." One other anecdote of his boyish days must suffice. It was the year before he entned college, at "Fasterns' E'en'' time (Shro,e Tuesday), when the married and ~irigle of Duns always joined in a game of handball. To every one's astonishmeut, Stephen joined in the contest, throwing himself into the match with much impetuosity, which led onlookers to say, "Is it possible ? Is that Steephie Hislop?" He came out of the fray a good deal mauled, and with a torn coat. It. had been his wont to speak of even trivial incidents, outside common cccnrrences, as under t11e direction of providence. "What a providrnce ! '' was his fa,ourite phrase. "Was your Fasterns' E'en fight a pro,idence ? " rnme one unkindly and incautiously remarktd. Looking hurt, he replied, "It was permitted." We pass over the many wanderings of the incipient naturalist over the mhny ample fields of the border country favourable for such pursni1 s, ramblings which he pursued upon the simple fare of coarse wbrnten Econe, or coarser barley bread, and the pure water from the burn or largu stream, with the addition, in the summer and autumn, of wild rasµberries, hips and haws, blackberries, and now and then, under prott:"st, the scrag-awle, or crab. Ha,i11g learned all that Duns could teach him, coming out first in Math~mlltic:s, Latin, and Greek, Stlphen entered the nniver~ity in bis se,enteenth year. T1 ,e " early piety" with which he entered the university did not receive much development during his four years in the Arts Faculty, bnt the mental training did him lasting service. In bis Divini1y course he had, first, three partiol sessions at Glasgow, and tben he returned to Edinburgh, and "came under the spell" of Cbalmeri; and Welsh, when he gave himself fully to study. He 611ppurted himself flS a schoolmaster, or as a private tutor, as many bad done before, and othe, s ha,e done since. We may quote Dr. Smith on the ha1,py state of things in the midst of which Hislop mored and bad his beiug : - " W bat they (Chalmers and Welbh) did for him at college was enlarged a, d prnctit·ally applied in the preaching of Dr. James Buchanan in the High Kirk. :Kot only the Church, but the whole land was Eeetbing with tbe eran1,:elical fe1vour, which, having gradually gained the ma,te1y in tl1e General AsEembly, resulted in the heroic eacrifice by

that mrijority which formed the Church of fLotla.nrl (Free) in 18+:C:. Hislop and the divinity stnrlents lived and debated, resrJlverl an l Hnffered, like their seniors dnrin~ the white heat of the Thir,l Reformation. He came out of college adrling to his s::ientific method anrl <levotion the love of tr11th, and a willingness to sacrifice evervthin,, for it, to;.{ether with consecration to Christ, and Christ alone, a:i Hearl (~f the Clrnrch, and King of the people given to him by the F,,ther, w~1ic\1 made him the great missionary he became." In Dr. Duucan, of R11thwell, he found a trne and sympathizing friend. The doctor's large scientific knowledge, and his fervent piety, no Jess than his evangelical preaching, drew Hislop to him. Thns hi;i summer residences as a tutor helped as much as they delighted him It was in 1841, while sWI a tutor, that he met the youn!:( lady God had designed ns his future wife and help-meet. Era~ma Hull came of a good evangelical stock. Her grandfather, Rw. Er-1gmus Middleton, was once Romaine's curate, a friend: of Top lady's, and preceded Leigh Richmond as rector of Tun·ey. Her father was the son of that Mr. Hull whom Whitefield commended to Newton when appointeu to Olney. It was from this town, rich with the memories of Cowper and Newton, Sutcliff and Carey, that he took his wife in due time. It is in his correspondence with Miss Hull that his religioui1 experience is told out. He had met with the saintly l\l'Cheyne, and had 1elt his influence, as he admired his zeal and devotion; but his f dl uecision-he called it his conversion-was reached through the instrumentality of Mr. Burns, who became the first Presbyterian Missionary to China. Hislop'~ devotion to missions was not the result of a lack of work at home. As his last term in divinity was closing at the university, amid the throes of the great Disruption, many competed for his stlrvices, for he was in the front rank of young men. The Blair Lidge School tempted him to become master and chaplain. Dr. Henry Duncan implored hirn to become his assistant and succe,sor; and one of the best livings iu the Established Church was offered him ; but he declined them all. While waiting to be licensed, he became secretary lo the Ladies' Society for Female Education in India, founded a few years before hy Major Jameson, a Bombay officer. He worked Eo hearWy for t1iat Society, that it proposed to send him out, when married, as a missionary to Bombay. Whib he wes waiting the direction of provideuce, Dr. John Wilson returned home accompanied by the fir~t Parsee conv, rt. Meeting with these gave a new impulse to his desire. l::lnt he had a humbling sense of his unfitness. Thus he wrote to his future wife : - ,, 20th January, 1843.-This morning, at our University i\Iissionary Association, we h~d a very interesting address from Rev. Dr. Stevenson, of Bombay. He told us of the need of missionaries in Iudia, and of the qualifications requisite in them. One qualification is a turn f :r languages, which I think I po~sess; but the most essential of all requisite~ in one who would do this work of the ernugdist foithfolly is personal piety-a singleness of heart and aim-increased devoteduess to Christ and his cause. In this respect-, I frankly acknowledge to you, I foll vastly short; and though I am deficient in courage and the tastti for busines~, it is in regarJ for spirituality of feeling that I am aw,irn

for the g-ift of the Spirit, that I may be spiritually fitted, (It least, for an_, department of the Lord's vineyard to which he may appear to send me." The adhesion of Dr. Duff to the Free Church gave a new impulse to the mis~ion-work of the infant society, and was a joy to all its adherents. ~otw1ths anding his O\\'n sense of unfitness, there was a growing sym- 1

pathy with the work, and an increased desire to enter upon it, which was ai<lerl ,ery much by the reading- of Dr. Duff's book, "Missions the Ci,ief End of the Church." On 20th January, 1844, he offered himself 1o the Foreign Missions' Committee of the Free Church, through Dr. Cordon, to go to India as a missionary. Among the committee there wa• a general appro,al of the canrlidate, but the decision was not taken f<>r a month. Indeed, the question was not whether he should go, but ithi'ther. A missionary was required for Nagpoor, the capital of what ::ire now called the Central Pro,ince'! of India; a candidate who had Leen under consideration was found not to be adapted to the very important work; as a consequence, Stephen Hislop was accepted as a man Hery way fitted for the µost. A .i,it to his brother Alexander, at Arbroath, nearly put an end to all these plans. Leaving Dundee, in the Wi'ndsor Castle, on the same <lay that the Queen's yacht left that port, the vessel strack apon a rock, and, when nearly filled with water, she struck on another. The compan_l' had been indulging in gay pastimes, and seemed to be wholly po,sesserl with passionate denunciation of the captain, giving vent to oaths anrl curse;; instead of cries fur help and mercy. As God would have it, , he second collision proved their rnlvation, for the ,essel was so fixer! t bat at low tide all escaped to the shore, in boats or otherwise. His marriage followed in due t.irne, and on November 3rrl, 18H, Stephen and Erasma Hislop lefL Southampton for Bombay. Narrowly c~caping shipwreck off the coast of Portugal, they reached Bombay 14th Dece111b«r. Nagpoor, which name is applied to the city and the surround ,ng district, denotes the serpent worship which marked the rcl,l!ion of its founders, the Gond tribes, the aboriginal inhabitants. It is a district rich in coal and iron, diamonds, and other precious stones, and _, et f11r thousands of years its inhabitants were little better than savages. It 1rns the part of India last of all to submit to invasion. Something rno, e than a century ago the J'ifaratha robbers overran its p!tiins, and 1:11 udnis,n and Mohammedanism followed, the Gonds taking very much tu th'" hills, dense forests, au<l jungles. .As early as 1810, Lieutenant (altcnrnrds Culond) Moxon took pity on the people. As commandant of the l{nideut's body-guard, be regularly addressed the Arab and Afghan tr, ,o ,0rs and sepoys, as also the Jliaratha-speaking peasantry. Hearing tl,at Dr. Carey was preparing a ~aratlii translation uf the Scriptures, he npplierJ fur copies. He afterwards went to Serampore, where he was IJ;,1itized, and wbere he married Miss Hobson, a niece of Dr. Carey.

He returned to Nngpoor with Marathi, Hindustani, and Hinrl11 Scriptures, and a native catechist. When, after some year8, Colonel Moxon retired, ond the Serampore mission ceased, the interee,sions of Lhe Moxons went up for Nagpoor. God heard their prayers ; and we find Sir Donald M'Leod, a civil Bervant of the East India Company, and a military officer, Sir William Hill, on the scene. Mr1xon, M'Leod, and Hill, from 1810, with a few years' break, until 1845, preparerl the way for Stephen Hielop, and the Central Indian Mission of the Free C ,nrch. Rev. A. Leslie, who led Henry Havelock to Christ, was made usetul to Sir Donald, and the Presbyterian became a Baptist. Of the GossnP-r mission to the Kohls, a similar tribe to the Gonds, at the instigation of Sir Donald, there is no space to speak. Sir W. Hill went to Madras in 1821, a thoughtless boy of six:reen. He fought throngh the firat Bnrmah war, when Judson suffered so sev.-,rely in his prison at Ava. He returned·to Kamtbi, nine miles from Nagpo,,r, after a visit home, and brought his young wife. They took their full swing of worldly pleasures for a time, until Lady Hill fell sick. Her eyes were opened ; a lady friend led her to Christ ; and as soon as she was able, she began to work among her native servants, and the young officers to whom she had access. When nursing a young s:ildier 1n a cholera visitation, she caught it, and died. In her last days she laid upon her husband the duty of devoting her fortune to the establishment of a Christian mission to the people of Kamthi and N agpoor. He was brought to Christ, and gave himself to him with full purpose of heart. He wrote to Dr. John Wilson, of Bombay, promising £2,500 for the establishment of a mission at Nagpoor and Kamthi. Stephen Hislop and his work was the outcome of this gift, and the faith and prayer which accompanied it. Hislop's co-worker here for eight years was Robert Hunter, who went out in response to the appeals of Dr. Duff. But in 1855, ill-health necessitated his return. He was in every way a congenial companion for Hislop, and has survived him, being- known in literature and science as Robert Hunter, LL.D., F.G.S. His brother Thomas was stationed as a miBsionary of the Established Chureh of Scotland in the Punjaub, where he founded the most spiritually fruitful of its missions. He, with his wife and child, were butchered in the mutiny of 1857. It would be interesting to give details of Hislop's work at Nai!poor, and of the Marathi converts which were given him. Of the first thr~e, one was arrested and brought to Christ by means of an exµosition of the history of Noah ; another was first impressed by a Tamil tract, "The Blind Way," which shows, by extracts from Hindu writings, the folly of idolatry. The third was a middle-aged farmer, who, while in a merchant's shop at Nngpoor, saw a strange-looking book, and bousrht it: it was a Marathi translation of a twopenny English primer for children, containing some of the words of Jesus Christ. He read it day by day. In his dreams at night he thought of the Saviour crucified for sinners. He abandoned idolatry, sanctified the Sabbath, gaYe up his caste observances, and received Christ as his Saviour. His conversion and baptism was the first stone of the Marathi cbureh. His name was Yadoji. The other two, who were Tamils, were named Monkhali and Virasawamy, or Virpa.

The field where Mr. Hislop lahoured was n difficult one, and in view of the dilHcnlties he learned the peculi~r helplessness of human iaslrumentality. He came in contact with Hindus prepossessed with the i-nperslition_ of ag~s ; ~ith Mussulma~s filled with contempt for every form of belief but their ou n; and with so-ca1ied Christians who had lc·arned 1o look upon all religions as alike. In addition to these things, the:e were ~':ils _strictly local and pnlitica!. " Thirty yee~·~," says Dr. S11,1t.h, '' British rnfluence liad bem tempenng Marathi misrule," and no ~1ission had clared to pe~etrat~ its 113,000 square miles of territory, and its nearly 12,000,000 of rnhab1tants. But here he laboured in preaching the ~o~pel, in edul'ation and other purely missionary work, with occasio,,al recrrati.e excursions in all dinctions in pursuit of objects dear to ,,aturalists, and in disconries as a scientist, all which, and especially the latter, were made to bear on the interests of his great work. In -visiting- the hills where the ahoriginal Gonds still hold their own, his heart was drawn out towards them as at once greatly needing evangel izaLion, and holding out encouraging prospects of unusual success, such as has been witnessed among the Kohls and Sanrhals. The deeply interesting work under notice gives facts from the journal of Mr. Hislop, which discover, more than anything written before, the real cause and methods of the terrible mutiny. It was Mohammedan in its c<•nception and plan, though the religious prejudices of the Hindus were utilized in the matter of the Cliapatees, 01· white wheaten cakes, "hich were mysteriously distributed from hand to hand, as if under tbe authority of the Go,erument. Nugpoor was one of the centres of revolt, and all the Europeans, civilians and military, were doomed. But God sa\'ed Nagpoor through Stephen Hislop, to whom the plot was revealed by Feiz Baksh, an old Mmsnlman gentleman, who came, under cover or the night, to Mr. H., with his son, a former pupil of the mission, and UJ g,-d him to make good his flight. The massacre was to take pl~ce at midnight, or in the early hours of Snnday, 13th June. By ten p.m. four hnndred fierce Mussulmans were lurking in the garden near the Mission-house. An agent was sent to the irregular ea.airy to join them ; but the native sergeant c.n duty was faithful, and when the agent was brought to him by the sentry, he committed him to prison, and gMve the a!Hrru to the European officers. Before midni~ht all had fled to Kamthi, or to a neighbouring fort. The bloodthirsty mutineers. ti11ding their plans abortive, and that their prey had escaped, made good their retreat. In 1858 Mr. Hislop visited his native land to recruit his exhausted energies. .As soon as he was convalescent., he set about forming a mi,sionary association in connection with erery Free Church congregatiun. He attended the Liverpool Conference, iu 1860, anJ on Saturday, ht December, the same year, he left London fur Nagpoor, pro,·eeding JJJ way of Folkestone, Paris, and Marseilles; and on the 26th of the same m,,nth, he and his wife were welcomed to the home of Dr. John Wilson, of Bum bay, who met them on the pier. All unconsciously on bis part, Mr. Hislop was used by God to bring about a much-needed reform in the entire civil admini,tratiou of Nagpoor, and to bring into existence the chief commis~io,,ership of the ~tu tral provinces, under officials of high perwnal character and equal energy and ability, the first of which \\'as Sir Richard Temple.

BTEI'HEN llISLOP.

When he returned to his loved work, he had leRs tlrnn three years to live, Jet, "into that brief period," says Dr. Smith, "he crowded the achievements of a life-time as effectually as if he had been told the measure of his days.'' Of him the lines were true : - " In secret love the Master To each one whispers low, 'I am at hand, work faster, Behold the sunset glow ! ' And each one smileth sweet Who hears the Master's feet." Mr. Hislop, like most other missionaries, did a good deal or itinerating in the cool sMson; and it was while out on a tour of in~pection of schools, and other iustituLions, with Sir Richard Temple, that the end unexpectedly came. Tbe party had reached the village of Bori, inhabited by shopkeepers, peasants, and dyers, on the Wana, near to which is a wooded hamlet named Takalghat, on a mound near the Krishna. It was on Friday morning when, after visiting tile native labourers, who were excavating the mounds, or ancient tumali, and taking a lata breakfast with the chief commissioner and Captain H. Mackenzie, that the missionary conducted family wnrilhip for the last time. He read 1 Thess. v., and prayed with remarkable fervout· anl unction, concluding by invoking God's blessing on all that had been done, and was oeing done, for the co aversion of the heathen in that lan,i. Af"er which, he dwelt M som'cl len~th on the effi.Jacy of the divine Word in convincing the human conscience. A storm which had come suddenly in the coarse of the day had swelled the little river Krishna to a flood, and it was in attempting to cross this on horseback after sunset-the stream which in the morning was a mere brook-that he lost his footing and was drowned, the horse escaping, and reaching Bori riderless. The river soon subsided, and he was fonnd in a sitting posture, with both hands clasping the turf by which he had in vain songht to regain the bank. In one pocket was bis Bible, and in the other some curiosities from one or the monnds. His death was a sad blow to Free Church Missions, and to all fellowworkers in the king<lom of our Lord, especially in India. But the work goes on, as also the institutions he founded-the Hislop Missionary College, the Native Christian Mission House, and varioL1s schools; and still we may say, "The servant dies, but the Master lives." Perhaps we could not conclude this paper better than by quoting passages from a letter addressed to Professor Duns, the friend to wbo[l), more than to any other, l-1e had been wont to unbosom himself. It describes so well what a missionary should be, aud what he so largely became, that it may be useful at this juncture when many young meu are devoting themselves to this noble work. It is dated 10th July, 1845 : - " When I think of all that the Redeemer has done for sinners, I do feel astonished that I shonld remain insensible to the amount of his love. And wheu I reflect on the freeness of his salvation, and my own career of carelessness and ingratitude, there is nothing on which I can place any confide ace s11ve on his finished and meritorious \\"Ork." . After other confessions, he adJs :-" I am c,mviuced that there 1s

draw ont a misrrable existence, there is no spirit-ual health, no soul prosperity; Rnd with it we are honourable as sous of the King of hea~en, :1~ princes hllving poll"cr to preniil with God. Aud if we prevail with God. we ~hall also prevail with men. Might in prayer is indeed the true secret of ministerial success.'' Wi)I not_ 1~1e Lord continue to raise u~ whole-henrted and capable men t,,r M1ss1on labour? Of course he will; and what if one of our readers, who has just read this article, should be predestinated to this high and h('annly calling-? l\Iay the suggesliou fall like a fire-flake into the heart of our fricncl !

"HE saved others, himself he cannot save." Such was the langnage hurled at Christ, in derision, by the rabble Jews who surrounded the cross and witnessed the dc~th of the Saviour of sinnerl'. But this sentence may be truthfully and well applied to Edgar George Wilson, the son of a Baptist minister, who lost his life while saving two lads who were drowning. He was, indeed, a hero ; one whose life was full of activity, and whose heart was filled with tenderness and love. He had, doubtless, learned many lessor:.s of i,elf-sacritice under the paternal roof, by what be had feen, heard, and experienced. I have heard of several praiseworthy deeds performed by this Baptist minister's son; bnt the one to which I would call your attention was his last act in life. It occnned on this wise. After partaking of his mid-day meal, while walking back to business by tbe river-side, he heard the cry of distress from Lwo little boys who had been fishing, and had fallen into the water. 'fhe river at this spot is between eight and nine feet deep. He gallantly. plunged in, and succeeded in bringing the boys safely to the bank. Unfortunately he was not a good swimmer himself. A student, who was in a boat near by, 1Yas attracted to the place by the cries of the boys, ~aw yo1;1ng Wilrnn's dangerons position, and threw his sculls to him; but he failed to grasp them, and sank to the bottom. When the body was reco,~red, it was noticed that one of the boy's fishing lines was twisted four times round the deceased's right wrist, and the hook had caught in . his clotLin!!, thus rendering his right arm powerlese. The news rapidly spread when it was too late to save his life. His parents were informed of the sad erent, which turned their home suddenly into a scene of great sorrow. In the midst of their trouble, a second son came home and witnessed the mourning of his mother. He inquired the meaning of his paren tb' distress, and EOon his heart and eyes were full also, as the cause of their grief was made kuown unto him. His brother! whom he lr,ved, and Lad seen so lately I Could it be possible he was dead? Yes, indeed, it was too true! '· Tell me, father," said tile second son, "how did my brother die ? ·what \\'as the cause of his death?"

" My boy," Paid the broken-hearted father, "your brother died tryin"' to save two little boys who had foll1cn into the river; and IV hen ) on; brother he11rd their cry of distress, he dashed into the water to try and s11ve them." '' And did he save them, father ? '' "Yes, my dear, he saved both the bo_ys, but was drowned himself." "Then," said the sorrowful son, as he brashed away, with his coatsleeve, t.he falling tears from his eyes, "I don't care a bit, then, now, father, if he sa,ed the boys." When the father told me this, I felt round to cry out, "Bravo, my boy! You must have sent a thrill of glow into that sorrowful homeste,cl by snch a noble expression amidst such a trying scene. Surely, both brothers were endowed with the same heroic nature. A few days later on, a crowd gathered together to pay the last tribute of respect at the grave of this noble yonng man. Pressing close up to the coffin came two little boys, in deep mourning, with a beautiful wreath of flowers in their hands, and tears in their eyes. They were t"o young to speak ; but their silent service that day, as they laid their tribute of love on the coffin in memory of their deliverer, touched the minister's heart; and this deed of gratitnde was an eloquent sermon of consolation to the bereaved fami1y in that hour of trial. It was touching to see this sorrowing Baptist minister turn from the bier that bore all that was mortal of his beloved son, and embrace each of the dear little boys that had been rescued from a watery grave at the price of his own boy; and after imprinting a kiss on each of their cheeks, he invoked God's blessing upon them for their future life. A local preacher, who witnessed this scene, was moved to tears, and went straight to his preaching-service and related what he had witnessed at the grave. He said-" Friends, I saw to-day what I shall never forget. I saw a man kiss two lads who were strangers to him, who had caused the death of his son." This statement arrested the attention of a man, who was a notable sinner in the place; and when the preacher said, "And that is just how God the Father will receive and welcome every sinner who comes to him, though they have caused the death of his only Son''; the man said to the local preacher, at the close of his service, " Will God kiss me Wee that ? " "Yes, indeed he will, if you come to him through Jesus Christ.'' "Then," said he, '' I will come to him at once ; '' and he did so. I was privileged to be in the city when the monument, erected to the memory of Edgar Wilson through the Y. M. C. A. of that place, was unveiled by the mayor, in the presence of a large crowd of onlookers. My friend, W. Y. Fullerton, took part in the public ceremony, and asked the divine blessing to rest upon all present, and prayed th,Lt some who had come to see the unveiling of the stone which marked the spot where a noble life had been sacrificed in rescuing others, might that day find the place and the occasion to be ordained for their salvation.
